title: Ast.parse mode='single' doesn't work as expected
author: NickC

text:
Mode ‘single’ is for single statements, not single lines.  It is intended for an interactive Python console or shell, as in the standard REPL and IDLE.  In single statement mode, the value of non-None expression statements get bound to ‘_’ and blank lines signal the end of compound statements.
In your example, you should parse multiline source_code as is.

author: duncathan

text:
Nick:

I need to ast.parse() line by line.


ast.parse parses legal python code, depending on the mode.  What is does with a line of non-Python code is somewhat undefined, but what it should do is raise an exception, preferably with a comprehensible message.



 Nick:

it appears that ast.parse() can’t [parse] a single line if statement.


Why do you say such that?  It parses single-line ‘if’ statements just fine.  You passed just part of one.  This is like, and if not caught would result in, calling .__init__ without a required argument.  The parser constructs a tree of instances of grammar classes.  The ‘If’ constructor requires a ‘body’ instance.  The error message says so.  See the entry for ast.If.
author: tjreedy

text:
Nick:

So it appears that ast.parse() can’t pass a single line if statement.


That’s correct (assuming you mean that you have just the condition with no body). The REPL does some minor hackery to figure out whether it has a complete statement or one that’s waiting on an indented block, and will take action accordingly; but there’s no way to compile if cond: on its own.
author: Rosuav

text:
Chris Angelico:

The REPL does some minor hackery to figure out whether it has a complete statement or one that’s waiting on an indented block


I believe the new REPL uses the hackery in codeop._maybe_compile that is invoked by the public functions in the same module.  One of these is called by code.interactive_interpreter, which IDLE uses.

text: @duncathan Because it needs to be done line by line so that the code modifications are done at the correctly time.  If it is done in a single batch then it will not fit in with other code modifications which are happening line by line.

author: duncathan

text:
Semi work-around now found but far from perfect because it fails if there is a comment after the if...: line.
import ast

source_code = \
"""x = 1;y = 2
if True:
    z = 3
"""
# <- ast fails: IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'if' statement

for line in source_code.splitlines():
    print(f"{line=}")
    pass_fix = False
    white_space = line[:(len(line) - len(line.lstrip()))]
    line = line.lstrip()
    try:
        tree = ast.parse(line)
    except IndentationError:
        print("pass_fix")
        pass_fix = True
        line += "pass"
        print(f"{line=}")
        tree = ast.parse(line)
    # print(tree)
    ast.fix_missing_locations(tree)
    modi_line = white_space + ast.unparse(tree)
    print(f"{modi_line=}")
    if pass_fix:
        modi_line = modi_line[:-9]
    modi_line = modi_line.replace("\n", ";")
    print(f"{modi_line=}")
author: NickC

text:
Assuming I understand the problem correctly, you might find a reasonable solution by considering the lineno and col_offset attributes of ast.AST instances (there are additional such attributes). Using ast.walk, you could accumulate instances in a dictionary whose keys are line numbers and perform the specific task against a k-v pair. This is just one approach.
On the other hand I have found myself wanting something like a path object that can provide the API of ast, but can “read” an input string character-by-character.
